hero.title: Body Fat Percentage Explained
hero.lead:
Your body fat percentage is the share of your total weight made up of fat, as opposed to muscle, bone, organs, and water. Two people can weigh exactly the same and have wildly different figures — which is precisely why this number tells you things the scale and the BMI chart cannot.

This guide covers the healthy ranges for men and women, how far you can trust each way of measuring it — the honest answer is less far than the display suggests — and how to use the number without letting it become another source of anxiety.

sections.heading: What body fat percentage actually measures
sections.html:
Body fat comes in two kinds, and only one of them is optional.

Essential fat is structural. It cushions organs, insulates you, and is required for hormone production, vitamin absorption, and reproductive function. Men need roughly 2 to 5 percent of body weight as essential fat; women need considerably more, around 10 to 13 percent, largely for reproductive health. Dropping below these levels is genuinely dangerous, not impressively lean.

Storage fat is the reserve — the layer under your skin (subcutaneous fat) plus the fat packed around the organs in your abdomen (visceral fat). Some storage fat is healthy and necessary. Visceral fat is the portion most strongly linked to type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, and it is also the portion that responds fastest when you become more active.

Body fat percentage combines all of it into a single figure, which is its strength and its weakness: it tells you how much fat you carry, but not where. That is why it pairs so naturally with a tape measure — see waist-to-height ratio, which speaks directly to visceral fat.

sections.heading: Healthy body fat percentage ranges
sections.html:
Unlike BMI, body fat ranges are sex-specific, because women carry substantially more essential fat than men. These are the widely used fitness-industry categories for adults.

Men

CategoryBody fatWhat it looks like
Essential fat2 – 5%The physiological minimum; not sustainable
Athletes6 – 13%Visible definition; typical of competitive sport
Fitness14 – 17%Lean and athletic-looking, maintainable year-round
Acceptable18 – 24%The healthy middle for most men
High25% and aboveCorresponds broadly to obesity; worth a doctor's input

Women

CategoryBody fatWhat it looks like
Essential fat10 – 13%The physiological minimum; not sustainable
Athletes14 – 20%Visible definition; typical of competitive sport
Fitness21 – 24%Lean and athletic-looking, maintainable year-round
Acceptable25 – 31%The healthy middle for most women
High32% and aboveCorresponds broadly to obesity; worth a doctor's input

Two caveats worth holding onto. Body fat naturally rises with age at a stable weight, so a 55-year-old and a 25-year-old at the same percentage are not in the same place — a few points above the "fitness" band in your fifties is unremarkable. And sitting very low for long periods carries real costs, particularly for women, where it is associated with disrupted or absent periods, bone density loss, and hormonal problems. Lower is not automatically better.

sections.heading: How the measurement methods compare
sections.html:
Every method estimates body fat rather than measuring it directly, and they disagree with each other — sometimes by a lot. Here is what each one is realistically worth.

MethodHow it worksTypical errorPracticality
DEXA scanLow-dose X-ray separates fat, lean tissue, and boneAbout 1 – 2 pointsClinic or sports lab; costs money; the practical gold standard
Hydrostatic weighingWeighed while submerged in waterAbout 2 pointsResearch settings only; you must exhale fully underwater
Air displacement (Bod Pod)Measures body volume in a sealed chamberAbout 2 – 3 pointsUniversity and sports facilities; quick and comfortable
Skinfold calipersPinch thickness at 3 to 7 sites, fed into a formulaAbout 3 – 5 points, skill-dependentCheap and portable; results vary a lot between testers
Tape measure (Navy method)Neck, waist, and hips plugged into an equationAbout 3 – 5 pointsFree, repeatable at home, no equipment beyond a tape
Smart scale (bioimpedance)Weak electrical current estimates lean massOften 4 – 8 points, sometimes moreEffortless daily use; heavily affected by hydration
Visual comparison chartMatching yourself to reference photosWide, but rarely worse than a bad scaleFree; surprisingly serviceable for tracking direction

The key thing about the bioimpedance scales most people actually own: the current travels more easily through water, so anything that changes your hydration changes the reading. Measure after a workout, after a salty meal, or dehydrated first thing in the morning and you can see swings of several points with no change in your body at all. That does not make the scale useless — it makes it a trend instrument rather than a measurement instrument.

sections.heading: Getting a number you can actually use
sections.html:
Because every home method has meaningful error, chasing accuracy is the wrong goal. Chase consistency instead: an imprecise method used identically each time still shows you the direction of travel correctly, and direction is what you want.

  • Use one method and stick to it. Comparing a caliper reading to a smart-scale reading tells you nothing except that the two devices disagree.
  • Standardize the conditions. Same time of day, ideally in the morning after using the bathroom and before eating or drinking, and not immediately after exercise. This matters even more for body fat than it does for weight.
  • Judge by the month, not the day. Real change in body composition happens over weeks. Day-to-day movement in a body fat reading is mostly hydration noise, the same phenomenon behind ordinary daily weight fluctuation.
  • Track it alongside weight, not instead of it. The interesting cases are when the two disagree — weight flat while body fat falls is exactly what recomposition looks like, and it is invisible if you only watch the scale.
  • Cross-check with a tape measure. Waist circumference is the single most reliable home measurement you can take, and it needs no formula or device.

None of this replaces BMI so much as it completes it. BMI is quick and universally understood but blind to composition; body fat percentage sees composition but is hard to measure well. Read together — plus a waist measurement — they rarely both point the wrong way at once. And if a home reading genuinely worries you, that is a question for your doctor, who can order a proper assessment rather than trusting a bathroom scale.

sections.heading: Tracking it: spreadsheet vs app
sections.html:
A spreadsheet handles this well. One column for the date, one for weight, one for body fat percentage, and a chart if you are willing to build one. That genuinely works, and if you already live in a spreadsheet, there is no reason to change.

What it costs you is the daily friction — opening the file, typing two numbers, and remembering to look at the chart. Records kept that way tend to be dense for three weeks and then stop, right before the period when the trend would have become readable.

The free Weight & BMI Feeltracker app is the low-friction version of that spreadsheet. It logs weight in kilograms or pounds, calculates BMI, and records body fat percentage alongside it, then charts all of them over any period with trend lines so a noisy daily reading does not read as progress or failure. It syncs with Apple Health, so a smart scale that already writes there can feed it, and syncs across iPhone, iPad, and Mac via iCloud with no account and no email address. Reminders keep the habit alive, widgets put the trend on your home screen, and you can export everything to PDF, XLSX, CSV, or JSON — including into a real spreadsheet, if that is where you wanted to be all along. Optional AI insights summarize what your own history has actually done.

Whatever you record it in, the discipline is the same: one method, same conditions, and patience with the number.

items.question: What is a healthy body fat percentage?
items.answer: Broadly **18 to 24 percent for men** and **25 to 31 percent for women**, with the leaner "fitness" bands sitting just below those. Both ranges shift upward slightly with age, and going far below them carries its own health risks.

items.question: Are smart scales accurate for body fat?
items.answer: Not as absolute numbers. Bioimpedance scales pass a small current through your body, and hydration changes the result — errors of 4 to 8 percentage points are common. They are still useful for tracking **direction** if you measure under identical conditions every time.

items.question: Is body fat percentage better than BMI?
items.answer: It answers a better question, but it is much harder to measure well. [BMI](/weight/bmi-chart/) is crude and precise; body fat is meaningful and imprecise. Most people are best served by watching both, plus a waist measurement.

items.question: How fast can body fat percentage change?
items.answer: Slowly. Real composition change shows up over weeks and months, not days — anything moving several points in a week is measurement noise, usually hydration. Expect to need at least a month of consistent readings before a trend means anything.

items.question: Can body fat be too low?
items.answer: Yes, and it is a genuine medical concern rather than an achievement. Below the essential-fat threshold the body cannot maintain hormone production; in women this commonly shows up as disrupted or absent periods and reduced bone density. If you are training toward very low levels, do it with medical supervision.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Home body fat measurements are estimates with wide margins of error and cannot assess your health on their own — always discuss body composition, weight targets, and any plan to change them with your doctor or healthcare provider. Seek medical advice if you are losing weight without trying, if periods stop or become irregular, or if very low body fat comes with fatigue, frequent illness, or stress fractures.
